Murray River near Wellington, south-east of Adelaide. Likely from Tailem Bend, 14 km upstream from Wellington, where the Ettrick Formation crops out (Pledge & Rothausen, 1977). "It is in this same area, just south of Tailem Bend, that the Ettrick Formation makes one of its few surface appearances, as a hard, pale greenish - grey, finely glauconitic marl (Ludbrook 1961 p, 38), occurring as a bench at present pool level of the river. This pool level is largely artificial, following the installation of barrages at the mouth of the river, in the 1930's, to control depth and salinity. It is therefore probable that the extent of outcrop of the Ettrick Formation was far greater circa 1880. Being glauconitic, and therefore of a somewhat reducing origin, the Ettrick Formation would yield teeth of a decidedly dark grey-black, colouration.

Murray River near Wellington, south-east of Adelaide. Likely from Tailem Bend, 14 km upstream from Wellington, where the Ettrick Formation crops out (Pledge & Rothausen, 1977). "It is in this same area, just south of Tailem Bend, that the Ettrick Formation makes one of its few surface appearances, as a hard, pale greenish - grey, finely glauconitic marl (Ludbrook 1961 p, 38), occurring as a bench at present pool level of the river. This pool level is largely artificial, following the installation of barrages at the mouth of the river, in the 1930's, to control depth and salinity. It is therefore probable that the extent of outcrop of the Ettrick Formation was far greater circa 1880. Being glauconitic, and therefore of a somewhat reducing origin, the Ettrick Formation would yield teeth of a decidedly dark grey-black, colouration.

"The Storm Creek section in Highwood Pass is located on the southwesterly flank of Mount Rae in the Misty Range, in a cirque which forms the source of Storm Creek, a principal headwater of Highwood River. The locality is most conveniently reached by way of the Kananaskis Highway [now highway 40], and lies immediately east of the summit of Highwood Pass (elevation 7,237 feet) at a point 45 miles south of Seebe, Alberta. From the road summit in the pass, a short walk east through open spruce woods encounters Storm Creek, a half hour ascent of which brings one to the cirque, above the timberline." The map in the publication lacked scale or lat and long reference marks. The lat and long were estimated from Google Earth based on the provided map and description.

From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

Absheron Peninsula, village of Dzhangi

Azerbaijan, “right bank of Sumgait River (Dzhengichai) three km northeast of Dzhengi guest house” (Mchedlidze, 1964 [1988:77], from Weber, 1928). Riabinin (1938:1 [Russian text], 173 [English summary]) stated that the remains of this animal were found “at the foot of an elevation located north of Sumgait River (Djenghi-Chai) at a distance of 3 km from the Djenghi Inn,” but Riabinin did not give his source for that information, which is somewhat different from that of Weber (1928). Mchedlidze (1976 [1984:1]) gave the locality as the “western part of Apsheronsk Peninsula, Dzhangi village.” We have not been able to determine the exact location of the Dzhengi guest house/inn; thus, the exact type locality remains uncertain. The most likely possibilities include outcrops in thePerekishkyul area, which have yielded many fossil whales (Mchedlidze, 1964), or outcrops along the Sumgait River just northeast of the town of Jangi, whose coordinates are 40 300 1000 W, 49 150 5100 E. When we initially looked into this ques- tion, we were confused by the reference to ‘Sumgait River (Dzhengichai)’ until we learned that the two names ‘Sumgait’ "and ‘Dzhengichai’ (also anglicized as ‘Jangichai’ from Azerbai- jani) both apply to the same river; ‘Dzhengichai’ being its name in the mountainous region west of the Apsheronsk Peninsula and ‘Sumgait’ after it enters the plain at the western margin of the Peninsula and flows northeastward to the coastal town of Sumgait (personal communication, Akif Alizadeh to A.E.S., 2 May 2012). Thus, the name ‘Sumgait River (Dzhengichai)’ means the Dzhengi portion of the river. We have also learned that Weber collected the remains of Mirocetus 15–20 km south-west of the city of Sumgait (pers. comm., A. Alizadeh to A.E.S., 2 May 2012) and, according to Weber (1928), on the right bank of the Dzhengi ( D Jangichai) River, and not on the Sumgait portion of the river as reported by Riabinin (Sanders & Geisler, 2015).

Ben Guerir area (Ganntour Basin, Morocco). From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

Ben Guerir area (Ganntour Basin, Morocco). From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

Gerdemann clay-pit, NW city of Gronau, Westphalia; R25 = 68740, H57 = 88080 on geological map Nordrhein-Westfalen
"Gerdemann & Co's brickyard list 1 km west from Gronau in Westphalia. The large, about 30 m deep outcrop, contains argillaceous slate of the Upper Wealden and the Valanginian. For a long time the brickwork outcrop has been known as a source of fossil vertebrates. Hosius mentions Gronau in the above-mentioned work as the source of an Iguanodon clavicula. The fossil is in the Münster Museum and is the distal part of the humerus or femur of a plesiosauroid of considerable size..." (Wegenr 1914, from a translation).

Ben Guerir area (Ganntour Basin, Morocco). From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

NOTE that this collection therefore represents sites that likely overlap a number of those recorded elsewhere, and would properly be listed under the acronym MAD (e.g. MAD98-01).

This site on Seymour Island (Isla Marambio in Spanish), Antarctica, was first discussed by Woodburne & Zinsmeister (1982), who discussed but did not name a polydolopid marsupial on the basis of specimens UCR 20910–20914. They did not name the site. Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) named the new genus and species _Antarctodolops dailyi_ on the basis of the same specimens and called the site RV-8200. Both abbreviations refer to the University of California at Riverside. According to Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984), the collection was made in the summer of 1982.

Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) give the coordinates as 64°13'S, 56°40'W, but these coordinates appear to be in the sea northwest of the island. Maps showing the location of were published by several authors, including Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984, fig. 1), Cione and Reguero (1994: fig. 2), Marenssi et al. (1994, fig. 2), Goin et al. (1999, fig. 1), and Chornogubsky et al. (2009: fig. 1).

This site is the type locality for _Antarctodolops dailyi_ Woodburne & Zinsmeister 1984, _Eurydolops seymouriensis_ Case, Woodburne & Caney 1988 (marsupials), and _Lyreidus antarcticus_ Feldmann & Zinsmeister 1984 (raninid crab).

To my knowledge, no in-depth review of all Seymour Island fossil sites has been published. Information in this collection is collected from passing mentions in general reviews and papers dealing with specific taxonomic group.

They did not name the site. Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) named the new genus and species _Antarctodolops dailyi_ on the basis of the same specimens and called the site RV-8200. Both abbreviations refer to the University of California at Riverside. According to Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984), the collection was made in the summer of 1982.

Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) give the coordinates as 64°13'S, 56°40'W, but these coordinates appear to be in the sea northwest of the island. Maps showing the location of were published by several authors, including Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984, fig. 1), Cione and Reguero (1994: fig. 2), Marenssi et al. (1994, fig. 2), Goin et al. (1999, fig. 1), and Chornogubsky et al. (2009: fig. 1).

This site is the type locality for _Antarctodolops dailyi_ Woodburne & Zinsmeister 1984, _Eurydolops seymouriensis_ Case, Woodburne & Caney 1988 (marsupials), and _Lyreidus antarcticus_ Feldmann & Zinsmeister 1984 (raninid crab).

From downtown Charleston, take Interstate 26 (I-26) north toward Columbia for 4.7 miles. Take exit 216A to merge onto SC-7 south/Cosgrove Avenue south, and continue south on SC-7 for 1 mile. Take first right on the south end of bridge; the parking lot is immediately adjacent to the west side of the bridge. Phosphate nodules and fossils can be found strewn across all muddy and sandy sediment surfaces at Northbridge Park. Collecting at low tide is best owing to greater exposure of the riverbank.

Take first right on the south end of bridge; the parking lot is immediately adjacent to the west side of the bridge. Phosphate nodules and fossils can be found strewn across all muddy and sandy sediment surfaces at Northbridge Park. Collecting at low tide is best owing to greater exposure of the riverbank.

Although the matrix containing the specimen described here (“cf. Pseudocorax sp.” of Shimada, 1997) is undoubtedly from the Smoky Hill Chalk of western Kansas and was likely collected by the Sternberg family in the early 1900s, the material lacks specific specimen information that would conclusively tie it with an existing KUVP number. Intriguingly, in 1911, Charles H. Sternberg (1911:72) noted: “Further, I have in my laboratory to-day a new species of shark, found this season on Hackberry creek whose vertebrae are half as large as the Lamna we secured. The teeth are so small that some of them can only be seen with a magnifying glass”. The description of the teeth appears to be consistent with that can be observed in KUVP 141876 (and the “Lamna” in Sternberg’s writing may refer to Cretoxyrhina). However, because KUVP 141876 as preserved does not contain any vertebrae, whether or not the shark specimen described by Sternberg (1911) and KUVP 141876 are the same specimen cannot be ascertained. It should be noted that ‘Hackberry Creek’ in this context implies southwestern Trego County, Kansas (Sternberg, 1911:71).

Situated near Road D64 in the county of Curnier, 8 km east of Nyons (Drôme, southeast France). The short succession crops out on the embankment of the forest track that climbs the "Fenestrelle" hill. N 44° 22' 53.89", E 5° 14' 59.94".

From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

Map sheet Bara 2C:26, Ed. 1987 (economic map "Gula Kartan" in Swedish, 1:20,000), coordinates 6165 1330. East of the village of Kvarnby, glacial rafts (Schollen) of a very pure white chalk are quarried by the Malmökrita AB company. The tilted Schollen are several hundred meters long and up to 30 m thick and are interbedded in a till. The rejected > 200 micron fraction is dumped into two abandoned quarries situated just west of Angdala Farm. Collected from the northwestern corner of the southern quarry, located immediately south of the sieving station.

Map sheet: Bubbarp 3D 7f, Ed. 1-Nov. 1975 (economical map, 1:10,000); coordinates 623722 137729. The western section (2 m east of the western limit of the quarry) exposed, from the bottom to the top, 1.15 m fine-grained calcarenite, 0.05 m cross-bedded sand, 0.65 m sandy calcisiltite with a basal conglomerate containing fist-sized phosphatized angular limestone fragments. The base of the conglomerate is used as reference level. On top of the Cretaceous is a 1.0-m-thick cover of Quaternary strata. The top of the Cretaceous part of the western section is situated 0.8 m below the corresponding level of the eastern section.

From phosphate mine east of Benguérir. The fossils were obtained partly by surface collecting in the trenches, but also on areas where the different phosphate levels are kept in stock separately and not mixed. During the mining process the different phosphate levels are removed in successive bearings, from the top down to the lowest Level 6, in broad and very long man-made trenches. Therefore, it has been possible to collect teeth in the successive levels, on very wide areas corresponding each time to a single level. Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

Furthermore, the phosphate extracted from a precise level is placed separately in storage areas, without being mixed with phosphate coming from other levels, avoiding thus mix-up or contamination. This particularity allowed us to collect numerous teeth on these stocks from identified levels, supplementing the samplings made in the trenches.

During the summers of 2003 and 2005, collecting trips were led to various localities in Greene County, including site AGr-43 (which exposes the Tombigbee Sand Member of the Eutaw Formation) and numerous gully sites near Clinton, Alabama (which all expose sections of Mooreville Chalk). Chalk is still present on the roots of all three specimens, indicating they were surface collected from the Mooreville Chalk exposures in the area. The ALMNH and MSC locality files record numerous gully sites in the area, making it unclear which particular locality the specimens were derived. As a result, the collecting localities for these specimens have been designated as AGr-Exp. 33 (2003 material) or AGr-Exp. 35 (2005 material). However, all the of the gully localities in this area are lithologically similar to site AGr-18 and are equivalent in age.

Manning Point on the northwestern coast of Hornby Island. Upon looking over the whole area it was discovered that lenses appeared here and there in the intertidal zone from high tide to low tide. The shale units show a lot of movement with various outcrops sorted and graded (e.g. finer shell fragments and tiny shark teeth, another having nothing but heavier Baculites shells), sometimes stacked as separate layers. This area, named "Hanging sheep", delivered a large fossil debris field that had been weathering a long time. GPS coordinates of the localities: HS MANN (= Hanging Sheep site at Manning Point): N 49°32'33.0" W 124°42'34.5".

The shale units show a lot of movement with various outcrops sorted and graded (e.g. finer shell fragments and tiny shark teeth, another having nothing but heavier Baculites shells), sometimes stacked as separate layers. This area, named "Hanging sheep", delivered a large fossil debris field that had been weathering a long time. According to de Greve (1938), the fossil collection from Iquitos comes from six different layers which are referred to in Table 1. The layers I, III, IV and VI were associated to the same outcrop section in the Telefunkenstation (telegraph station) site (de Greve, 1938), while layers II and V cropped up in other two different sites along the banks of the Itaya River. So far, no vertebrate specimens in the Iquitos collection has been associated either with layer V. Two other layers, including one from the lignite bank, and one of indeterminate location from Itaya (Table 1), were not referred to by de Greve (1938). From these we could not find any invertebrate/ vertebrate remains associated to the layer of indeterminate location from Itaya. In contrast, from the lignite bank layer, labelled as Telefunkenstation (blue in Table 1), which is referred to here for the first time as “layer VII”, abundant fish remains, and coprolites are identified (Table 2). According to de Greve (1938), there was a bone-bed layer between the two main lignite layers at the Telefunkenstation site, which was characterized by abundant bone splinters and fish remains. The lignite bank layer VII contains abundant fish remains and bone fragments that could suggest a match with the bone-bed layer referred to by de Greve (1938). Although some specimens in the collection do not have precise information about the layer from which they come from (referred to in Table 2 as indeterminate locality), their taphonomic and preservation conditions could suggest that these specimens likely were collected in any of the layers that cropped up in the Telefunkenstation site.

The nowadays abandoned quarry that produced the pavestones is located near the settlement of Vatsiana (34˚48'56.69"N; 24˚6'21.50"E), but the fossiliferous horizons are largely covered in debris. Marly limestones that have been quarried to produce slabs used as pavestones in at least two locations; the lighthouse (Faros) and Aghia Triada Chapel. Slab extraction directly from the fossiliferous horizons did not yield any identifiable remains, possibly due to low fossil concentration, but several identifiable specimens were recovered from the debris of past quarrying activity. Most of the better-preserved specimens were embedded in slabs used as pavestones around the lighthouse.

Africanaspis fossils were initially collected during excavations by RG, between 1993 and 1995
from a thick layer (up to 6 meters) of laminated black shale lenses near Grahamstown, in the
Eastern Cape Province of South Africa. This layer was exposed in 1985 during construction of
the N2 road bypass, in a cutting at Waterloo Farm (33˚19’24.88"S, 26˚32’12.70"E) (Fig 1). Following collapse of the cutting in 1999, 30 cubic metres of the shale was removed by hand during stabilisation of the road cutting. These were transported to a storage facility and have
allowed for continued meticulous excavation to reveal the fossils. In 2006 a further collapse occurred allowing the removal of additional fossiliferous material to the storage facility, facilitated by the National Roads Agency. All Africanaspis material has been recovered from the ‘main fish lens’ (MFL), which has been the prime source of vertebrate material.

The Akkermanovka locality is located in the south of the Orenburg Oblast (Southern Urals, Russia), about 2 km northeast of Akkermanovka and 15 km southwest of the city of Orsk (51.20516 N 58.24972 E). The Akkermanovka locality comprises two large adjacent quarries, referred to as the central quarry ("Tsentralny"), and the northern quarry. The central quarry is well known for its Carboniferous (upper Visean) deposits, which are considered an important Lagerstatte for Carboniferous invertebrates (Mychko et al., 2019). Within the Carboniferous limestones of the quarry, deep incisions and caverns secondarily filled with Cretaceous (and probably also Palaeogene) sediments are preserved (Mychko et al., 2019). Unfortunately, no reliable biostratigraphic or lithographic markers have yet been reported from these palaeodepressions (“palaeocaves”), thereby rendering their precise chronostratic ages as ambiguous (Mychko et al., 2019). The new material described here was recovered from one of these "palaeocaves" in the central quarry. The locality represents an area of several tens of square meters with two Upper Cretaceous outcrops of loose terrigenous sediments at the edge of the road comprising a large (up to 5mthick) primary outcrop and a less prominent (about 2 m) secondary outcrop. The upper layer which possibly connected these two horizons has been destroyed by weathering and therefore it is unknown if these two palaeodepressions were infilled during a single event or at separate intervals.

The sample was collected during a recent expedition aboard E/V
Nautilus that explored the deep-sea geology and biology around
Johnston Atoll (NA141; June 19-14 July 2022). The tooth was collected on a dive using the ROV Hercules at a depth of 3090 m on an unnamed seamount located ~350 km southeast of Johnston Atoll (Dive H1926, 14.11332°N, 167.39357°W, 23 June 2022), within the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument. The ROV dive during which the sample was collected surveyed a narrow ridge that runs in a southwest to northeast direction for about 5 km with slopes on the ridge crest averaging about 20 degrees.

records.ggc: In order to ensure adequate water supplies during periods of low rainfall and drought, a 17 km long pipeline was planned for laying from a pumping station at Buckland (TQ227516) through to a natural reservoir at Outwood (TQ328453). The pipeline was due to cross the lower part of the Lower Cretaceous outcrop in the area. TB monitored the progress of the trench and noted that the area south of Wonham Mill (TQ2240 4962) had the potential to expose the otherwise rare Atherfield Clay Formation. A modest 30-40 metre section was temporarily exposed at TQ225493 (circa 51°13'46.67" N, 0°14'47.48"W) and access was granted by Clancy Docwra to sample the discharged material upon the easement prior to its return to the trench for backfilling; direct access into the trench was not permitted.

Bletchingley quarry (TQ 3290 5029) was located just south of Bletchingley village in Surrey. The quarry was owned by Hall Aggregates, part of the RMC group. Extraction of sand was started by the company in the early 1960s near Mitchener's Bank (TQ 3370 5016), and subsequently progressed westward towards Outwood Lane. This paper concerns the microvertebrate fauna collected from the northern pit (TQ 3290 5029).

The provenance of specimens indicated on the original label (Levico) is certainly problematic, given that sedimentary cover is virtually absent in that area and outcrops consist exclusively of Variscan basement rocks. A transcription error regarding the locality name on the label can likely be ruled out, as "Levico" also appears on the label of two *Ptychodus* teeth housed at MUSE in Trento (cat. no. 5115). It is possible that the "Levico" designation simply refers to the main town near the fossil discovery sites. If so, the specimens most likely originate from the nearest Cretaceous "Scaglia" outcrops, located approximately 5 km west [most likely should be east] of Levico on the right bank of the Brenta River.

The village of Rudawa, located almost halfway between Zabierzów and Krzeszowice, is the westernmost locality in the Kraków region where Cretaceous layers are exposed. The bottom of the Rudawa River flowing in this place, below the chalk bedrock, descends in a stepped manner, forming prominent steps, repeated several times at irregular intervals. Fossils collected from these steps.

The village of Rudawa, located almost halfway between Zabierzów and Krzeszowice, is the westernmost locality in the Kraków region where Cretaceous layers are exposed. The bottom of the Rudawa River flowing in this place, below the chalk bedrock, descends in a stepped manner, forming prominent steps, repeated several times at irregular intervals. Fossils collected from these steps.

In the lowest places, right at the mouth of the streams into the Rudawa valley, on both sides of the valley, exposed layers older than the Senonian, overlying Jurassic limestone, are visible. Right next to the road leading from Trojanowice to Giebułtów lies the lowest bed of Cretaceous conglomerate.

The chondrichthyan material discussed in this paper was collected from the bed and banks of the Ouachita River northwest of Malvern, Arkansas. The exposure from which our specimens derive is of small areal extent, less than 2,000 m2 of riverbed. The chondrichthyan fauna occurs almost entirely as isolated teeth scattered across the exposure surface by the Ouachita River.

The Mirebeau region (Vienne, western France) has some remnants of Tertiary sediments preserved from erosion. The majority of outcrops in the region are Cretaceous and Jurassic sediments. At the place called "Le Moulin Pochard" there are some old open workings in a Middle Miocene (Langhian) sand lens directly eroding into a Cenomanian substrate. "Le Moulin Pochard" is southwest of Mirebeau, near Amberre, and coordinates based on location labeled "Falunières de Moulins Pochas".

At the place called "Le Moulin Pochard" there are some old open workings in a Middle Miocene (Langhian) sand lens directly eroding into a Cenomanian substrate. "Le Moulin Pochard" is southwest of Mirebeau, near Amberre, and coordinates based on location labeled "Falunières de Moulins Pochas".

The specimen comes from an uncertain locality at Santa Cruz province, Argentina. Ischyodus crassus fossils were part of a lot including shark teeth that were sold to the British Museum in August 1899 by R.F. Damon (1845–1929). Several specimens came from localities like ‘Río Chubut’, ‘Santa Cruz’ and ‘Monte Deseado’. Although there is no certainty about who collected the specimens, Vizcaino et al. (2016; see also Vizcaíno and Bargo 2013) mentioned other fossils originating from the area commercialised by R.F. Damon were probably collected by Handel T. Martin (1862–1931) expedition. However, the specimens discussed herein were obtained previous to the work of Handel T. Martin in Santa Cruz province, and thus it is unlikely that they were collected by that expedition.

Bahia Nueva, Chubut province, Argentina. Cione (1988), is the first author that recognized that the type specimens of E. pozzii came from Bahía Nueva (as can be seen in the label of the type specimens). Cione suggests that this locality is located between the Chubut River valley and Trelew city (Cione, 1988). However, the port of Bahia Nueva, also known as "de las Ollas" port by the end of the 19th century, corresponds to the coastal area of Puerto Madryn (see Caviglia, 2011). Consequently, the type locality of Echinorhinus pozzii should be considered as the neighborhood of Puerto Madryn city.

A location on the left bank of the Bulungu, about 2.5 km from the river bank [from map, Bulungu river appears to extend only ~1 km from the Congo]. At this location, the highly weathered limestone is transformed into a type of marly clay, which the natives use as pottery clay. It was in the quarries created to extract this clay that the fish remains were discovered. Some fossil descriptions imply that "River Bulungu" and "pottery clay excavations" are different localities (and Onchosaurus pharao only mentions pottery clay excavations) but the locality section only mentions fish fossils coming from one locality.

This region is called "Buala Bemba" by the natives, and the existence of this lake, Lake Yanga, has long been known. The southeast side of the lake has numerous small rocky hills.

Fausse Pointe-Noire (Goyo-M'Vassa). This beautiful deposit is located on the coast, south of Pointe-Noire. It forms a small cliff a few meters high, and the formation of more resistant rocks defines a small point extending into the sea. This point extends into underwater outcrops, indicated by the presence of a wreck that ran aground on the reefs.

Not far from the road from Landana to Lela, near the indigenous village of Kama M'Bote, are numerous rocky outcrops. Large boulders appear in particular in the bed and on the bank of the small Samvo stream, located about 1 km east of the village, 20-30 meters northwest of the road. The river bank, about 5 to 6 meters high, shows the rock in place, but the cross-section is quite difficult to discern due to landslides and tangled vegetation.

The border post of Ifassabe has been relocated. It is currently located near the indigenous village of Chicarnba. Not far from this location, in the village of Chibuete, there is an outcrop of fossil-bearing rocks. This outcrop is located on the bank of the Chimagne stream, in a patch of primitive forest that extends from this point to near the lagoon. There, it forms a wall about 3.5 meters high, visible for about a hundred meters and then disappearing beneath the recent terrain.

About 4.5 km north of the mouth of the Shiloango, the coast, low until then, rises into two small cliffs: the Chinchoxo Cliffs. These cliffs consist of two hills separated by an Avicennia backwater; their height does not exceed 20 meters. In the second cliff (1 km to the north), this clay is only visible over about ten meters and has an average thickness of 1 to 1.5 meters, but it is laden with fairly abundant coprolites and contains some fish remains (mostly shark teeth).

The Bololo deposit is located near the confluence of the Bola River, not far from the ancient village of Bololo, in the lower center of geodetic signal J. 12. The edge of the plateau reveals, beneath about ten centimeters of blackish soil, a thick layer of reddish sandy clay, clearly visible in deep and steep erosional ravines, and showing quartz pebbles and lateritic concretions scattered irregularly throughout the mass, especially abundant at the base. Below, on a small hill jutting out towards the south and overlooking the marshes to the west, rocky outcrops appear; towards the west, this hill slopes gently towards the Bola River. Point 1 is located 1 km east of the village of Bololo, at the point where the hill slopes gently, about 6 m above the level of the Bola.

In the desert area between Shiloango and the Landana motor road, in the Borna Tate region, lies a large plain, marshy in the rainy season, with a lake that persists even in the dry season. This region is called "Buala Bemba" by the natives, and the existence of this lake, Lake Yanga, has long been known. The southeast side of the lake has numerous small rocky hills.

Fausse Pointe-Noire (Goyo-M'Vassa). This beautiful deposit is located on the coast, south of Pointe-Noire. It forms a small cliff a few meters high, and the formation of more resistant rocks defines a small point extending into the sea. This point extends into underwater outcrops, indicated by the presence of a wreck that ran aground on the reefs.

South of the Manzadi indigenous chiefdom (Zadi-Kakongo) are numerous and very diverse outcrops, often highly fossiliferous. Outcrops located in the vast area below and to the south of the Manzadi plateau, a sort of depression occupied by an irregular series of small hills arranged in a bizarre manner and without any apparent order. Points 3 and 4 are located on the left and right sides of a small dry valley more or less parallel to the river, about 1.5 km west of point 2.

South of the cliffs at point Luvula, recent rockfalls, colored clays, black alum-bearing clays, gravelly sands, and cross-stratified sands, again obscure the section. In places, however, enormous isolated boulders, sometimes fossiliferous, can be observed on the beach. These blocks were mainly observed in the vicinity of Beta m'Bembe and Matumbo (n'Tumbo).

The Bololo deposit is located near the confluence of the Bola River, not far from the ancient village of Bololo, in the lower center of geodetic signal J. 12. The edge of the plateau reveals, beneath about ten centimeters of blackish soil, a thick layer of reddish sandy clay, clearly visible in deep and steep erosional ravines, and showing quartz pebbles and lateritic concretions scattered irregularly throughout the mass, especially abundant at the base. Below, on a small hill jutting out towards the south and overlooking the marshes to the west, rocky outcrops appear; towards the west, this hill slopes gently towards the Bola River. Point 4 is the extreme part of the promontory towards the river formed by Bololo Hill.

All the fossil material was recovered within the 1.25 km linear distance along the south side of the Red Deer River in Dorothy, Alberta, Canada (51° 16' 29"N, 112° 19' 43"W to 51° 15' 57"N, 112° 19' 5"W). Most of the specimens were collected in situ from five microvertebrate sites concentrated within a 150 m diameter (DSnail, MSnail-1–MSnail-3, and TSnail). Fossils from those microsites were first collected through dry, bulk sampling of the matrix on site, approximately 100 kg in total mass, which was then screen washed with microsieving (No. 20/0.841 mm mesh) at the museum. TMP 2011.048.274 and TMP 2011.048.291 were surface collected approximately 560 and 1240 m southeast from MSnail-1, respectively, with MSnail-1 constituting the northernmost collection site.

This site on Seymour Island (Isla Marambio in Spanish), Antarctica, was first discussed by Woodburne & Zinsmeister (1982), who discussed but did not name a polydolopid marsupial on the basis of specimens UCR 20910–20914. They did not name the site. Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) named the new genus and species _Antarctodolops dailyi_ on the basis of the same specimens and called the site RV-8200. Both abbreviations refer to the University of California at Riverside. According to Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984), the collection was made in the summer of 1982.

Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984) give the coordinates as 64°13'S, 56°40'W, but these coordinates appear to be in the sea northwest of the island. Maps showing the location of were published by several authors, including Woodburne and Zinsmeister (1984, fig. 1), Cione and Reguero (1994: fig. 2), Marenssi et al. (1994, fig. 2), Goin et al. (1999, fig. 1), and Chornogubsky et al. (2009: fig. 1).

This site is the type locality for _Antarctodolops dailyi_ Woodburne & Zinsmeister 1984, _Eurydolops seymouriensis_ Case, Woodburne & Caney 1988 (marsupials), and _Lyreidus antarcticus_ Feldmann & Zinsmeister 1984 (raninid crab).

To my knowledge, no in-depth review of all Seymour Island fossil sites has been published. Information in this collection is collected from passing mentions in general reviews and papers dealing with specific taxonomic group.
Locality 2 (RV-8424,64°14' 12"S, 56°39'45"W) is on the north ridge at the mouth of "Breakwind Canyon". Stratigraphically it is about 10m upsection from locality 1.

Locality 4 (RV-8262, 64”15’15“S, 56’41’37”W) is on a small cuesta on the south side of the Cross Valley drainage, overlooking both the main drainage and the major southern drainage. Stratigraphically it is in unitTelm 2, about one-third to half-way up the section.

Locality 5 (RV-8266, 64°14'50"S, 56°41'05"W) is on the south side of the toe of the major ridge that separates the Cross Valley and “Breakwind Canyon”. It is on a small ridge that separates Cross Valley from the small drainage between the two larger drainages.

During the summers of 2003 and 2005, collecting trips were led to various localities in Greene County, including site AGr-43 (which exposes the Tombigbee Sand Member of the Eutaw Formation) and numerous gully sites near Clinton, Alabama (which all expose sections of Mooreville Chalk). Chalk is still present on the roots of all three specimens, indicating they were surface collected from the Mooreville Chalk exposures in the area. The ALMNH and MSC locality files record numerous gully sites in the area, making it unclear which particular locality the specimens were derived. As a result, the collecting localities for these specimens have been designated as AGr-Exp. 33 (2003 material) or AGr-Exp. 35 (2005 material). However, all the of the gully localities in this area are lithologically similar to site AGr-18 and are equivalent in age.

The 600 m long stretch of the Conecuh River that we studied is in the NW1/4, SW1/4, Sec. 35, T5N, R15E (River Falls 7.5: quadrangle topographical map). Three locations along the creek were intensively worked during four separate field visits. These sites, herein identified as "X", "Y" and "Z", were selected based on the exposed thickness of the section containing the vertebrate fossil-bearing deposit. The initial collection site, "X", is located at the northern-most extent of the outcrop (31.359281 lat., -86.519598 long.), whereas "Y" and "Z" are located at 31.358868 lat., -86.520317 long., and 31.358378 lat., -86.521518 long., respectively. Bulk matrix was processed at all sites. [Specimens not assigned to individual sites in the paper]

The small fossil deposit is located 300 m from the Montaldo tower, in an ESE direction and can be characterized, with an approximation of 10 m according to the U.T.M. system, by the coordinates MQ15425779. Access is via the departmental road n° 119, descending about sixty meters on the path which starts from the road at the bend which is near the votive pylon dedicated to San Michele. When the left edge of the path breaks off to open onto an orchard, it is easy to notice the presence of fossil shells that indicate the outcrop of geological strata. These exhibit a very different appearance and composition on the two sides of the path.

Access is via the departmental road n° 119, descending about sixty meters on the path which starts from the road at the bend which is near the votive pylon dedicated to San Michele. When the left edge of the path breaks off to open onto an orchard, it is easy to notice the presence of fossil shells that indicate the outcrop of geological strata. These exhibit a very different appearance and composition on the two sides of the path.

In Nations 1975: "Material from excavation at southeast corner of North Pacific Avenue and Hards Street in San Pedro, collected at the approaches to Vincent Thomas Bridge connecting San Pedro and Terminal Island." In Fitch 1970: "During construction of the western approach for the Vincent Thomas Bridge, the hill (terrace) on the east side in the 700 block North Pacific Avenue was cut down and hauled away." Hards Street no longer exists, but the remnant is the northern entrance to the present-day Harbor Occupational Center, and corresponds to the 700 block.

Poggio delle Bandite near Vitaleta (municipality of San Quirico d'Orcia, province of Siena; WGS84 [World Geodetic System 1984] UTM reference 32TQN1471). Unfortunately, the site where the teeth were found no longer exists. It was levelled in the 1980s for land reclamation for agriculture, like many other Tuscan badlands rich in "biancane" (small dome-shaped hills) and "calanchi" (hydrographic units with steep bare slopes).

The rock block containing GMNH-PV-3227 (Figure 1) was obtained by Ishii, one of the authors, from an acquaintance residing in Hokkaido (the collector of this specimen). Ishii subsequently donated it to the Gunma Prefectural Museum of Natural History, where it is now a stored specimen (GMNH-PV-3227). Currently, contact with the collector has been lost, so the detailed location and specific geological context of the find are unknown. However, through the communication Ishii had with the collector when acquiring the specimen, it is known that the collector was active in collecting specimens primarily around the Shuparo River area. Ammonite fossils with similar color and lithology to the matrix containing GMNH-PV-3227 have been found in the Shuparo River basin. Based on these points, it is highly probable that the block containing GMNH-PV-3227 was collected in the vicinity of the Shuparo River basin.

Map sheet Bara 2C:26, Ed. 1987 (economic map "Gula Kartan" in Swedish, 1:20,000), coordinates 6165 1330. East of the village of Kvarnby, glacial rafts (Schollen) of a very pure white chalk are quarried by the Malmökrita AB company. The tilted Schollen are several hundred meters long and up to 30 m thick and are interbedded in a till. The rejected > 200 micron fraction is dumped into two abandoned quarries situated just west of Angdala Farm. Collected from the northwestern corner of the southern quarry, located immediately south of the sieving station.

Most fossils from the site have been either dug out of or picked up from the roadbed of the new extension of Highway 45,about seven miles south of Booneville, near the community of Frankstown, in western Prentiss County, northeastern Mississippi. Going north, the road crosses the top of a hill, passes over Twenty Mile Creek, then runs over a raised roadbed above the flood plain of the creek, a low area called Twenty Mile Bottom. The fossils appeared suddenly at the site during the summer of 1990 because of the building of the road. The road construction crew cut off the top of the hill south of the creek and used it as fill for the the raised roadbed on the north side. The roadbed was made available to Booneville High School students and fossil collectors from April 22 to May 2,1991, to study and collect. It was later graded and the roadside was covered with soil and seeded with grass.

Most fossils from the site have been either dug out of or picked up from the roadbed of the new extension of Highway 45,about seven miles south of Booneville, near the community of Frankstown, in western Prentiss County, northeastern Mississippi. Going north, the road crosses the top of a hill, passes over Twenty Mile Creek, then runs over a raised roadbed above the flood plain of the creek, a low area called Twenty Mile Bottom. The Scheerders van Kerchove (SVK) clay pit, referred to by Janssen (1981) as 'nieuwe groeve' (new quarry), is situated about 1.5 km SW of the centre of Sint-Niklaas (province of Oost-Vlaanderen, Belgium). The temporary pits dug in order to reach this base, were situated in an imaginary circle with parameters r = 100.00 m, mx = 133.190 and my = 204.830 (Lambert co-ordinates, National Geographic Institute, 1998; topographic map of Belgium, sheet 15/5-Noord, Sint-Niklaas). With the logistic support of the directors of the Scheerders van Kerchove’s verenigde fabrieken, however, collaborators of the Gemeentelijk Natuurhistorisch en Heemkundig Museum Grobbendonk (GNHMG) dug temporary pits in 1999, 2000 and 2001 to expose the base of the Boom Clay Formation. This enabled the excavation of 300 m2  and wet-sieving down to 1.0 mm mesh of an equivalent of about 50 m³ of this basal deposit.

Most previous Miste digs were organised on a field owned by the Berenschot family. It is located a couple of hundred meters to the northeast of the 2013 dig site described here. In 2004, the Berenschot property was changed into a lovely park. Therefore, it was impossible to organise any more digs on that terrain. For the 2013 dig, we had to look at other possible locations. From the literature (Janssen, 1984), we knew that the Miste Bed was accessible in a field owned by the Brethouwer family. Thanks to their participation, we were able to manually drill a test borehole on their field into the Miste Bed. That showed us that the fossils preserved in the Brethouwer field were of high quality. Therefore, we decided to organise the 2013 dig in that field. WGS84 coordinates 51.93264, 6.66518.

The few specimens mentioned in this note all come from the excavation work for the new Kallo sea lock, on the left bank of the Scheldt (Beveren Map - 27 E). These specimens were collected by washing and sieving sediments taken primarily from two points, specifically in the immediate vicinity of points 27 E 150 (sample 1) and 27 E 175 (sample 2) on the said map. These points correspond to the location of exploratory boreholes, preliminary to the construction of this new port complex. Sample 1 (approximately 800 liters) was taken midway between the two boreholes recorded under number 27 E 150 in the Geological Survey Archives, and sample 2 (approximately 500 liters) approximately 50 meters south of borehole 27 E 175.

Based on the content of the small label, it is determined that the larger of the two specimens was collected at Tenjin-yama in Nishishikada - formerly part of Kasakake Village, and now located in Nishishikada, Kasakake-cho, Midori City. The section regarding Tenjin-yama in the article "Kasakake Village in the Stone Age (Part 1)" (Iwasawa, 1938; p. 9) - published in Vol. 5, No. 1 of *Keno*, a journal edited by Shosaku - contains the following description: "A single fossilized shark tooth - locally referred to as a 'Tengu's Claw' - was discovered."

There is currently no place name within the Chichibu region that exactly matches the name inscribed on the specimen's label. However, a relatively similar place name exists - Kanasaki in Minano-machi, Chichibu-gun, Saitama Prefecture - suggesting the possibility that Shosaku collected the specimen in that vicinity. Approximately 2.1 km southwest of Kanasaki - upstream along the Arakawa River in the vicinity of Obuchi - strata corresponding to the lower section of the Akabira Group (a Neogene formation constituting the Chichibu Basin) are exposed. From a geological perspective, this suggests that these strata are the most probable source layer from which this fossil specimen originated.

The fossil was found near an artificial cliff constructed at the boundary between the African Zone on the north side and the American Zone on the south side of Gunma Safari Park. This cliff is an artificial outcrop created by repurposing geological strata exposed from beneath the soil during the park's landscaping work. According to Shigehisa Kawakami, the director of the park, the fossil was not directly found at this outcrop, but rather was found lying beneath the outcrop, separated from the fossil itself. However, since herbivores are kept free-roaming in these zones and the general public is not allowed to enter except for the animal care staff, it is considered highly unlikely that fossils were brought in from outside.

The 600 m long stretch of the Conecuh River that we studied is in the NW1/4, SW1/4, Sec. 35, T5N, R15E (River Falls 7.5: quadrangle topographical map). Three locations along the creek were intensively worked during four separate field visits. These sites, herein identified as "X", "Y" and "Z", were selected based on the exposed thickness of the section containing the vertebrate fossil-bearing deposit. The initial collection site, "X", is located at the northern-most extent of the outcrop (31.359281 lat., -86.519598 long.), whereas "Y" and "Z" are located at 31.358868 lat., -86.520317 long., and 31.358378 lat., -86.521518 long., respectively. Bulk matrix was processed at all sites. [Specimens not assigned to individual sites in the paper]

The Enseada I archaeological site is a shellmound located at Babitonga bay on the island of São Francisco do Sul, on the north coast of Santa Catarina state, Brazil. The site is located next to the Enseada bay and was heavily disturbed by anthropic actions before its excavation in the year of 1969 to obtain raw material to pave roads and make fertilizer. More than 100 shellmounds have been recorded in Babitonga Bay (Fossile et al., 2019, 2020).

The Rio do Meio shallow site is located at Jurerê beach, north of Santa Catarina Island, Brazil. It was identified in 1987 and excavated in 1996 and 1997. Two main areas were excavated by natural layers: RM I and RM II, with 448 m2. The site is situated on the waterfront in a dune area with dense vegetation of restinga, which is delimited at the east and west by an elevation of Precambrian rocks, still covered by a Neotropical rainforest, and by a mangrove at the south (Fossari, 2004).

The provenance of specimens indicated on the original label (Levico) is certainly problematic, given that sedimentary cover is virtually absent in that area and outcrops consist exclusively of Variscan basement rocks. A transcription error regarding the locality name on the label can likely be ruled out, as "Levico" also appears on the label of two *Ptychodus* teeth housed at MUSE in Trento (cat. no. 5115). It is possible that the "Levico" designation simply refers to the main town near the fossil discovery sites. If so, the specimens most likely originate from the nearest Cretaceous "Scaglia" outcrops, located approximately 5 km west [most likely should be east] of Levico on the right bank of the Brenta River.

The majority of the excavations from which fossils were obtained are close to the top of the escarpment between 31°52'50" N, 4°50'00"W and 31°49'46"N, 4°57'22"W. Additional excavations occur along a river gorge close to the site where the measured section of Kennedy et al. (2008) was studied at 31°51'45"N, 4°56'32"W.
